definition.text: Unexpected, unusual, severe or unseasonal weather at the far ends of the range a place has seen in the past.

facts.text: The main types are heat waves, cold waves, droughts, and heavy rain or storms such as tropical cyclones.
The IPCC treats an event as extreme if it is as rare as or rarer than the 10th or 90th percentile of observed weather.
Severe weather, which threatens life and property, is one kind of extreme weather.
Natural climate variability, such as El Niño, explains some extremes, but system-wide changes can raise their frequency or intensity.
Warmer air holds more moisture, so storms can drop more rain and cause floods and landslides.
Paving land and destroying wetlands, which store water naturally, can worsen floods.
Death tolls from natural disasters have fallen over 90 percent since the 1920s even as population quadrupled.
A global study found drought and extreme heat cut national cereal production by 10% over 1964–2007.

definition.text: The monetary losses that extreme weather events cause to economies.

facts.text: A 2023 study put climate-change-driven extreme weather costs at about US$2.86 trillion over 2000–2019, roughly US$143 billion a year.
The IPCC estimated in 2011 that annual losses since 1980 ranged from a few billion to above US$200 billion, peaking in 2005, the year of Hurricane Katrina.
Losses of lives, cultural heritage and ecosystem services are hard to monetize, so loss estimates reflect them poorly.
In the 2023–2024 World Economic Forum risk survey, 66 percent of respondents named extreme weather a top risk.

definition.text: Research that works out how far causes such as climate change explain trends in extreme weather events.

facts.text: A single extreme event generally cannot be blamed on any one cause.
Much of the work relies on climate models, which are vital but only approximations.

definition.text: A measure of how much a change, such as more greenhouse gas, shifts the balance of energy flowing into and out of the atmosphere.

facts.text: Greenhouse gases, aerosols, surface albedo and solar output all change Earth's energy balance.
It is measured in watts per square meter, usually averaged over the whole globe.
A planet in radiative equilibrium has zero net forcing and a steady equilibrium temperature.
The IPCC puts human-caused forcing at 2.72 [1.96 to 3.48] W/m2 in 2019 relative to 1750, mainly from greenhouse gases, partly offset by aerosols.
For CO2 the forcing is roughly ΔF = 5.35 × ln((C0+ΔC)/C0) W/m2, so each further increase warms less.
The 50% rise in CO2 since 1750, as of 2020, corresponds to a forcing of +2.17 W/m2.
It lets the warming effect of different drivers, such as different greenhouse gases, be compared.
Effective radiative forcing removes rapid atmospheric adjustments unrelated to long-term surface warming.

definition.text: A number, in kelvin per W/m2, that links a radiative forcing to the eventual change in surface temperature.

facts.text: It is the inverse of the climate feedback parameter.
A value of about 0.8 gives about 1.6 K of warming since 1750 from CO2 rising from 278 to 405 ppm, a forcing of 2.0 W/m2.
The same value predicts a further 1.4 K of warming if CO2 doubled from its pre-industrial level.

definition.text: The fraction of incoming sunlight that Earth reflects back to space, about 0.30 (30%) on annual average.

facts.text: Clouds, aerosols, oceans, land, snow, ice and vegetation reflect sunlight; Earth absorbs the other 70%.
Deforestation typically raises reflectivity, while Arctic ice loss lowers it.

title: Carbon dioxide in the atmosphere
article: Carbon dioxide in the atmosphere of Earth

definition.text: Carbon dioxide (CO2) is a trace gas in Earth's air that plays a central part in the greenhouse effect, the carbon cycle and photosynthesis.

facts.text: It is one of the three main greenhouse gases in Earth's atmosphere.
In 2026 its concentration reached 432 ppm (0.0432%), a 54% rise from the 280 ppm of the 10,000 years before the mid-18th century.
The rise is caused by human activity, mainly burning fossil fuels, with cement making, deforestation and biomass burning adding more.
Human emissions exceed what natural sinks can absorb; about half of the CO2 from fossil fuels stays in the air.
By 2024 humans had emitted an estimated 2,650 gigatonnes of CO2 since 1850, at 42 gigatonnes a year; about 1,050 gigatonnes remain in the air.
A projected 20–35% of fossil carbon released so far will keep CO2 levels raised for many thousands of years.
Today's concentration is the highest for 14 million years.
Regular measurements at Mauna Loa began in 1958, building on Dave Keeling's accurate flask samples of the 1950s.

title: CO2 fertilization effect
article: Carbon dioxide in the atmosphere of Earth#CO2 fertilization effect

definition.text: The speeding-up of plant photosynthesis, with less water lost through leaves, caused by more carbon dioxide in the air.

facts.text: Its strength depends on plant species, temperature and the water and nutrients available.
It has been reported to cause 44% of the increase in gross primary productivity since the 2000s, and Earth's land has greened markedly since the early 1980s.
Faster photosynthesis does not always mean more growth or carbon storage, and plants are unlikely to cut CO2 levels much over the next century.

title: Main greenhouse gases
article: Greenhouse gas#Contributions of specific gases to the greenhouse effect

definition.text: The gases that do most of the heat-trapping in Earth's atmosphere: water vapour, carbon dioxide, ozone, methane and nitrous oxide, plus clouds.

facts.text: Without the natural greenhouse effect Earth's surface would average about −18 °C instead of around 15 °C.
Water vapour causes about 50% of the greenhouse effect and clouds about 25%, but these change with temperature, so they are treated as feedbacks.
CO2 (about 20%), tropospheric ozone, CFCs and nitrous oxide change independently of temperature, so they count as external forcings.
Of human greenhouse gas emissions in 2019, equal to 59 billion tonnes of CO2, 75% was CO2, 18% methane, 4% nitrous oxide and 2% fluorinated gases.
Methane comes from livestock, wetlands, rice, landfills, coal mining and oil and gas; nitrous oxide mostly from microbes breaking down fertilizer.
Methane lasts about 12 years in the air on average, while CO2 lasts much longer.
By 2022 CO2 concentrations had risen about 50% and methane 164% since 1750.
In the IPCC table, nitrous oxide lasts 121 years with a 100-year GWP of 265; some fluorinated gases, such as SF6 at 23,500, are far stronger.

title: Water vapour feedback
article: Greenhouse gas#Special role of water vapor

definition.text: The process in which warming lets the air hold more water vapour, a greenhouse gas, which adds further warming.

facts.text: Water vapour causes 41–67% of the greenhouse effect, but people do not directly change its global level.
It stays in the air only about nine days, so local changes such as irrigation have little global effect.
Physics (the Clausius–Clapeyron relation) means warmer air holds more water vapour per unit volume.

title: Observed global warming
article: Climate change#Warming since the Industrial Revolution

definition.text: The rise in Earth's average surface temperature measured since thermometer records reached global coverage around 1850.

facts.text: Datasets agree that surface temperature is rising by around 0.2 °C per decade.
The 2016–2025 decade averaged 1.26 °C [1.13–1.36 °C] above the 1850–1900 baseline, and 2024 was more than 1.5 °C above.
Up to 1970 there was little net warming because sulfur dioxide pollution, which reflects sunlight, offset greenhouse warming; after that, warming sped up.
Warming is measured as a 20-year average because natural variability can make a single year 0.2 °C warmer or colder.
Over 90% of the extra heat since 1970 has gone into the ocean.
Land has warmed almost twice as fast as the global average, and the Arctic three to four times faster than the rest of the world.
Other signs include retreating glaciers, heavier rain, earlier spring flowering and thousands of species moving to cooler areas.

definition.text: Estimates of how much hotter Earth will get, which depend mainly on future greenhouse gas emissions.

facts.text: The IPCC expects the 20-year average to pass +1.5 °C in the early 2030s.
By 2100 warming is very likely to reach 1.0–1.8 °C with very low emissions, 2.1–3.5 °C with intermediate emissions, or 3.3–5.7 °C with very high emissions.
In the intermediate and high scenarios warming continues past 2100.
The remaining carbon budget, the CO2 that can still be emitted for a given temperature limit, comes from modelling the carbon cycle and climate sensitivity.
UNEP says a 50% chance of staying below 2.0 °C allows 900 gigatonnes of CO2 after 2023, about 16 years of current emissions.

title: Causes of recent warming
article: Climate change#Causes of recent global temperature rise

definition.text: The drivers behind today's warming, which scientists identify by comparing the 'fingerprints' of each possible cause with observed patterns.

facts.text: Natural cycles such as El Niño cause short-term spikes and dips; longer changes come from external forcings like greenhouse gases, the Sun, volcanoes and Earth's orbit.
The Sun is ruled out: its energy reaching Earth has shown no upward trend since 1880, and the upper atmosphere is cooling rather than warming.
Volcanic CO2 equals less than 1% of human emissions, and natural forcings have had negligible effect on temperature trends since the Industrial Revolution.
Human activity, mainly burning coal, oil and gas, has raised greenhouse gas levels since the Industrial Revolution.
Aerosols from air pollution have a smaller cooling effect, and land use change so far has slightly cooled the planet by making surfaces more reflective.
Land sinks remove about 29% of yearly CO2 emissions and the ocean absorbed 20 to 30% over the last two decades.

definition.text: A representation of the physical, chemical and biological processes that shape the climate system, used to project future warming.

facts.text: Models are tested by checking how well they reproduce present and past climates.
Past models underestimated how fast Arctic ice would shrink and rainfall would increase.
Some models add population, economic growth and energy use to produce emission scenarios that feed physical and carbon cycle models.
Depending on the scenario, they give CO2 concentrations ranging from 380 to 1400 ppm.

definition.text: A measure of long-term warming from doubled CO2 that also includes slow feedbacks, such as melting ice sheets and changing vegetation, which take millennia.

facts.text: These slower feedbacks make it larger than equilibrium climate sensitivity, possibly twice as large.
It is estimated from Earth's geological history, so future values are highly uncertain.

title: Effects of climate change

definition.text: The well-documented and growing impacts of climate change on the natural world and on human societies.

facts.text: Changes include a warming trend, shifting rainfall patterns and more extreme weather, with fiercer fires, thawing permafrost and desertification.
Some changes can become irreversible once tipping points are crossed.
Oceans and ice sheets absorb most of the extra heat, delaying effects that then continue after surface temperatures settle; sea level rise is a major long-term concern.
Mountains, coral reefs and the Arctic are the most immediately threatened ecosystems; at 2 °C about 10% of land species would become critically endangered.
For people, food and water supplies, health, farming, fisheries and forestry are at risk, and heat stress will limit outdoor work in the tropics.
Poor people, children and Indigenous peoples are especially at risk, and rich industrialised countries, which emitted most CO2, have more resources to adapt.
Wealthy colder countries have felt little economic harm or even gained, while poor hot countries probably grew less than they would have.
Damages rise with temperature: one comparison found total damages at 1.5 °C were 90% lower than at 3.66 °C.

related: Global economic costs of climate change

definition.text: The ways climate change harms human health, from heat illness and worse air to disease spread and extreme weather.

facts.text: Longer exposure to high temperatures can cause heat illness and heat-related deaths.
Diseases spread by mosquitoes and ticks, such as dengue fever and malaria, may become more common in some regions, as may waterborne diseases.
Lower crop yields can raise food prices and cause undernutrition, and clean water supplies can shrink.
Together these can increase poverty, migration, violent conflict and mental health problems.

definition.text: The threat climate change poses to growing, reaching and relying on enough food.

facts.text: Causes include higher CO2, heat, changed rainfall, more extreme events and shifting pests and diseases.
Disasters from extreme weather caused food production losses estimated at US$123 billion in 2025, 5% of global agricultural GDP.
It is projected to harm all four pillars of food security, affecting how much food exists, its price and quality, and how stable supply is.
Ocean biomass is expected to fall by about 5% per degree of warming, hitting tropical seas hardest.

title: Climate-sensitive economic sectors
article: Effects of climate change#Highly affected sectors

definition.text: The parts of the economy most exposed to climate change because they depend directly on weather: farming, fishing, forestry, tourism and energy.

facts.text: Thermal power plants need cooling water and run less efficiently when hot, while hydropower suffers when river flows fall.
Heat, lower water flow and changed rainfall could cut total energy production by 7% a year by the end of the century.
Insurance premiums, such as for flood cover, are rising, and Munich Re warned in 2019 that home insurance could become unaffordable for average-income households.
Above 1.5 °C of warming, tourism and outdoor work may reach limits to how far they can adapt.

related: Global economic costs of climate change

title: Ice sheet decline
article: Effects of climate change#Ice sheets decline

definition.text: The melting of the Greenland and West Antarctic ice sheets, which will keep raising sea levels over long time-scales.

facts.text: Losing the whole West Antarctic ice sheet would raise sea level by over 5 metres, and a partial collapse could be abrupt and irreversible for centuries or longer.
Sustained warming between 1 °C and 4 °C would melt the Greenland ice sheet entirely over millennia, adding 7 m to sea levels.
As the ice surface melts it gets lower and warmer, a self-reinforcing feedback that can make the loss irreversible.

related: Tipping points in the climate system

definition.text: How much Earth's surface will warm in response to a doubling of the carbon dioxide concentration in the atmosphere.

facts.text: Warming triggers climate feedbacks, such as melting ice and more water vapour, whose strength is not known exactly.
Doubling CO2 gives a forcing of about 3.7 W/m2, which without feedbacks would cause roughly 1 °C of warming.
In 1990 the IPCC put equilibrium sensitivity between 1.5 and 4.5 °C; observations and physics now give a very likely range of 2.3 to 4.7 °C.
Because mitigation costs depend on how fast carbon neutrality is needed, sensitivity has large economic and policy consequences.
One study suggests halving the uncertainty in the transient climate response could save trillions of dollars.
If sensitivity is high, the Paris goal of well below 2 °C cannot be met, at least temporarily.

definition.text: A measure of how much heat a greenhouse gas traps over a set period compared with the same mass of carbon dioxide.

facts.text: By definition CO2 has a GWP of 1.
A gas's GWP depends on how strongly it absorbs heat radiation, how fast it leaves the air, and the time frame chosen.
Methane has a GWP-20 of 81.2 but a GWP-100 of 27.9, because it leaves the atmosphere much faster than CO2.
Regulators usually use a 100-year time scale, and international agreements have adopted it as the standard.
Since 1997, Kyoto Protocol reporting has used fixed IPCC GWP values to convert gases into comparable CO2 equivalents.
Other metrics include the global temperature change potential and GWP*, which treats short-lived pollutants such as methane differently.

conflicts.text: The 2021 IPCC report lists methane's GWP as 83 over 20 years and 30 over 100 years.
conflicts.note: Same 2021 IPCC report quoted as 81.2 (GWP-20) and 27.9 (GWP-100) in the lead; possibly fossil vs non-fossil methane values.

definition.text: The mass of carbon dioxide that would warm the Earth as much as a given mass of another greenhouse gas.

facts.text: It gives one common scale for the climate effects of different gases.
It is calculated as GWP times the mass of the gas: two tonnes of a gas with GWP 100 equal 200 tonnes CO2e.
Values depend on the time scale chosen, usually 100 or 20 years.
Carbon markets and carbon taxes price emissions per tonne of CO2 equivalent.

definition.text: The warming of a planet's surface that happens when heat-trapping gases in its atmosphere stop it losing heat to space.

facts.text: Sunlight passes through greenhouse gases to heat Earth's surface, which gives off longwave heat radiation that the gases mostly absorb.
Without this absorption Earth's surface would average −18 °C; with it, the average is about 15 °C.
Adding greenhouse gases through human activity strengthens it, which is called the enhanced greenhouse effect.
The rise in radiative forcing from human activity has been observed directly and is mainly due to more atmospheric CO2.
Joseph Fourier proposed the effect as early as 1824, and Eunice Newton Foote showed in 1856 that CO2 strengthens solar warming of air.
The name comes from greenhouses, though these keep heat mainly by blocking moving air rather than by absorbing radiation.

definition.text: A gas in an atmosphere that traps heat and so raises the surface temperature of a planet such as Earth.

facts.text: Greenhouse gases absorb the heat radiation a planet gives off, which produces the greenhouse effect.
Nitrogen and oxygen, 99% of dry air, barely absorb heat radiation, while CO2, methane and nitrous oxide, under 0.1% of the air, do.
Water vapour causes 41–67% of the greenhouse effect, but human activity does not directly change its global level.
Most human CO2 comes from burning fossil fuels, plus cement, fertilizer and land-use change such as deforestation.
Emissions reached an all-time high of 53.6±5.2 Gt CO2e per year over 2014–2023.
In 2022 the IPCC warned emissions must peak before 2025 and fall 43% by 2030 for a good chance of limiting warming to 1.5 °C.

definition.text: Releases of greenhouse gases from human activities, which strengthen the greenhouse effect and drive climate change.

facts.text: Carbon dioxide from burning coal, oil and natural gas is the main cause of climate change.
Global emissions are about 50 Gt a year and were estimated at 57.7 Gt CO2eq for 2024.
The power sector contributes about 27%, transport 15%, and industrial energy and agriculture 11% each.
Emissions began rising with fossil-fuelled industry around 1750 and grew rapidly after about 1950.
China emits the most each year, followed by the United States, which emits more per person.
Average emissions of 4.9 tonnes per person a year are over twice the 2.3 tonnes consistent with the 1.5 °C goal.
2015 was the first year with both global economic growth and falling carbon emissions.

title: Climate change

definition.text: Present-day climate change is global warming, the ongoing rise in Earth's average temperature, together with its wider effects on the climate system.

facts.text: It is driven by human activity, chiefly burning coal, oil and gas since the Industrial Revolution, plus deforestation and some farming and industrial practices that release greenhouse gases.
The atmosphere now holds roughly 50% more carbon dioxide than at the end of the pre-industrial era.
2024 was the warmest year on record, at +1.60 °C since regular tracking began in 1850.
It brings more flooding, extreme heat, food and water scarcity, disease and economic loss, and the poorest communities, who emitted least, are the most vulnerable.
Under the 2015 Paris Agreement nations agreed to keep warming 'well under 2 °C', yet current pledges would still lead to about 2.8 °C by 2100.
Warming can be limited by cutting emissions and by removing carbon dioxide from the air; as of 2019 carbon pricing covered about 20% of global emissions.
Joseph Fourier proposed the greenhouse effect in the 1820s, and climate change reached international public attention in the late 1980s.
